1. Introduction

Best known today as a philosopher and historian of the sciences, Alexandre Koyré was a broadly trained philosopher, with interests across the Western tradition. Footnote 1 He wrote works on theology, Plato, Descartes and German mysticism, as well as studies of Galileo and Newton, and the two books he is probably best known for today – From the Closed World to the Infinite Universe and The Astronomical Revolution . Footnote 2 Koyré was born in Russia, attended lectures in France by Henri Bergson and in Germany by both Edmund Husserl and Martin Heidegger.

FROM THE CLOSED WORLD

TO THE INFINITE UNIVERSE

(Du Monde clos à l'Univers infini)

PAR
A. KOYRÉ

L

A philosophie et la science du moyen âge connaissaient un cosmos délimité et bien structuré, qui devint, aux xvi e et XVII e siècles, le monde des modernes, — un univers infini sans l'ombre d'une structure hiérarchique. Cette transformation fondamentale est décrite dans cet ouvrage ayec les termes mêmes des philosophes et savants de cette époque. L'auteur va de Nicolas de Cuse aux travaux de Copernic, Bruno, Kepler, Descartes, Newton et Leibniz.

...

Plusieurs chapitres sont consacrés au problème de l'origine des concep- tions newtoniennes, et à la réaction des contemporains de Newton, tels Berkeley, Raphson et Leibniz. L'accent est mis, d'un bout à l'autre du livre, sur le rapport étroit qui unissait alors pensée scientifique et pensée philosophique, sur leurs influences réciproques.
Le livre de M. Koyré éclaire brillamment la période où le monde occidental subit une révolution profonde qui transforma notre manière de penser et qui aboutit à la science et à la phi- losophie modernes.

Koyré’s book surveys the understanding of the “size” (finiteness, volume, or definiability thereof) of the universe through notable European thinkers in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. During the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries a radical change occurred in the patterns and the framework of European thought. In the wake of discoveries through the telescope and Copernican theory, the notion of an ordered cosmos of "fixed stars" gave way to that of a universe infinite in both time and space—with significant and far-reaching consequences for human thought. Alexandre Koyré interprets this revolution in terms of the change that occurred in our conception of the universe and our place in it and shows the primacy of this change in the development of the modern world.
